summary: Specifies how IS-IS carries IPv6 routing information using two new TLVs: a reachability TLV and an interface address TLV. With these, one intra-domain routing protocol can route IPv6 together with IPv4 and OSI. It is on the standards track and has been updated since.

eli5.summary: IS-IS first learned to talk about older internet addresses. This teaches it to also describe the newer, longer kind, so a single set of routers handles both.

subtitle: How IS-IS learned to carry IPv6 prefixes with two new TLVs, so one routing protocol can handle IPv6, IPv4 and OSI.

tldr.problem: IS-IS already routed OSI and IPv4, but it had no way to describe IPv6 prefixes or IPv6 interface addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two TLVs (an IPv6 Reachability TLV, type 236, and an IPv6 Interface Address TLV, type 232) and a new IPv6 protocol identifier, 142.
tldr.outcome: One intra-domain routing protocol can route IPv6 along with IPv4 and OSI. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7775.

today: RFC 5308 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7775. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Extending IS-IS for IPv6
sections.content:
IS-IS is an extendible intra-domain routing protocol. Each router in the routing domain issues a Link State Protocol Data Unit (LSP) with information about that router. The LSP holds typed, variable-length data called TLVs (type-length-values).

RFC 1195 describes how to route both OSI and IPv4 with IS-IS. This RFC reuses that method with minor changes. It defines two new TLVs, "IPv6 Reachability" and "IPv6 Interface Address", and a new IPv6 protocol identifier. The new TLVs use the extended metrics and up/down semantics of RFC 5305.
sections.eli5: Routers already trade notes in a fixed format. This RFC just adds two new kinds of note so they can talk about the new addresses too.

sections.title: The IPv6 Reachability TLV
sections.content:
The IPv6 Reachability TLV is TLV type 236 (0xEC). It is the IPv6 equivalent of the two IP reachability TLVs in RFC 1195 (internal and external), with an "external" bit in place of two separate TLVs.

It describes reachability by giving a routing prefix and metric information. It also carries an up/down bit (U), an external bit (X), a bit saying whether Sub-TLVs are present (S), and optionally the Sub-TLVs themselves for later extension. It MAY appear any number of times, including none, within an LSP. Link-local prefixes MUST NOT be advertised with it.

The prefix is packed: only the needed octets are present, computed as the integer of (prefix length + 7) / 8. If the Sub-TLV bit is 0, no Sub-TLV octets follow. If it is 1, the octet after the prefix holds the length of the Sub-TLV part, and Sub-TLVs have the same type, length, value form as ordinary TLVs.
sections.eli5: Each reachability note says "you can get to this neighborhood through me, and here is how costly it is." It only writes down as much of the address as it needs.

sections.title: Up/Down Bit, External Bit and Metric
sections.content:
As RFC 5305 says, the up/down bit SHALL be 0 when a prefix is first injected into IS-IS. If a prefix is advertised from a higher level to a lower level (for example level 2 to level 1), the bit SHALL be 1, meaning the prefix has traveled down the hierarchy. Prefixes with the bit set to 1 may only be advertised down the hierarchy.

If a prefix was distributed into IS-IS from another routing protocol, the external bit SHALL be set to 1. The RFC notes this is useful when distributing prefixes from IS-IS to other protocols.

As in RFC 5305, a prefix advertised with a metric larger than MAX_V6_PATH_METRIC (0xFE000000) MUST NOT be considered in the normal Shortest Path First (SPF) computation. This allows a prefix to be advertised for purposes other than building the normal IPv6 routing table.
sections.eli5: One flag says "this note already went down a level, do not send it back up." Another says "I heard this from someone outside the club." A really huge cost means "do not use this for directions."

sections.title: Interface Address TLV and the IPv6 NLPID
sections.content:
The IPv6 Interface Address TLV is TLV type 232 (0xE8). It maps directly to the "IP Interface Address" TLV of RFC 1195, except that it holds 0 to 15 interface addresses of 16 octets each, instead of 0 to 63 four-octet IPv4 addresses.

Its meaning depends on where it is advertised. In Hello PDUs it MUST contain only the link-local IPv6 addresses of the interface sending the Hello. In LSPs it MUST contain only the non-link-local IPv6 addresses assigned to the IS.

The IPv6 Network Layer Protocol ID (NLPID) is 142 (0x8E). As with IPv4, an IS that supports IPv6 routing using IS-IS MUST advertise this in the "NLPID" TLV.
sections.eli5: A router lists its own addresses in a note. Addresses that only work on one wire go in the greeting. Addresses that work everywhere go in the big map update. It also says out loud that it speaks IPv6.

sections.title: Path Metrics and Route Preference
sections.content:
The prefix processing follows the same changes to RFC 1195 that RFC 5305 made, and both concern the SPF calculation. Because the metric space is larger, the original MAX_PATH_METRIC (1023) is redefined as MAX_V6_PATH_METRIC, the same value as in RFC 5305 (0xFE000000). If a path metric would exceed it during SPF, it SHALL be treated as that value.

The order of preference between paths to the same prefix MUST take the up/down bit into account. From best to worst it is: Level 1 up, Level 2 up, Level 2 down, Level 1 down.

If several paths tie on preference, the choice is made by metric. Remaining ties SHOULD be considered for equal-cost multi-path routing if the router supports it. Otherwise the router can pick any one of them.
sections.eli5: If there are several ways to reach the same place, routers have a ranking for which kind of note to trust first. Then they pick the cheapest route, and if there is still a tie they may split traffic or just pick one.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA updated the IS-IS codepoint registry so TLV codes 232 and 236 refer to this RFC. It also created a new registry for Sub-TLVs of TLV 236, with a Type range of 0 to 255. Allocations require documentation of the use and approval by the Designated Expert assigned by the IESG. All codepoints are currently unassigned.

The RFC says it raises no new security considerations. Security considerations for IS-IS are covered in ISO 10589 and in RFC 5304.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list where new sub-notes get registered, and it starts out empty. The RFC says it adds no new safety worries beyond what IS-IS already has.
